_comment: TEMPLATE — the command path below is a PLACEHOLDER and must be replaced. SessionStart hook that fires the nexus cold-boot recovery trigger when the orchestrator session is brought back (matcher 'resume' covers `claude --resume` AND `claude --continue` — the chaperon's bring-back path at boot). Merge the `hooks` block below into your orchestrator's settings.json under $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR (do NOT replace an existing `hooks` object — splice SessionStart into it), replacing <YOUR_NEXUS_ROOT> with your own NEXUS_ROOT. `async: true` keeps the hook from blocking session start; boot-recover.sh additionally backgrounds the heavy recovery, so it returns within milliseconds regardless. THEN RUN `monitor/boot-recover-hook-check.sh` — see _why_placeholder. See monitor/README.md -> 'Cold-boot recovery trigger'.
_why_placeholder: This file used to ship one operator's absolute path (your-org/nexus-code#1174). Copied verbatim onto another host that path does not exist, and Claude Code reports the failure ONLY on channels nobody is looking at. Measured against 2.1.246 with a positive control that fired: stdout, stderr and the exit code are byte-identical to running with NO hooks at all, for both `async` settings and both the `startup` and `resume` matchers. It IS recorded in three places -- the session transcript (no flags needed: one extra `attachment` of subtype `async_hook_response` carrying hookName, hookEvent, stderr and exitCode 127; `async: false` is louder still, `hook_non_blocking_error`, carrying the command verbatim), `--output-format stream-json --verbose` (`hook_started` + `hook_response` with outcome "error"), and `--debug-file` (an explicit "Hook SessionStart:startup (SessionStart) error:"). None of the three is on by default. So an unreplaced placeholder is exactly as invisible in practice as a wrong absolute path -- #1174's suggestion that a placeholder makes a verbatim copy fail VISIBLY at the first fire does not hold. The placeholder is therefore necessary (a reader cannot mistake it for a working value) but NOT sufficient, and the thing that is actually loud is a check outside the session: monitor/boot-recover-hook-check.sh. Run it after wiring the hook and treat its exit code as the evidence that recovery is armed. A CAUTION FOR WHOEVER RE-MEASURES THIS: an earlier version of this note claimed "completely silent, --debug included", on the strength of a `--debug` arm that was an EMPTY INSTRUMENT -- `--debug` routes nothing in `-p` mode, so its 160 bytes name no hook in EVERY arm INCLUDING THE WORKING ONE. The positive control proved the HOOK fired; it could not prove the INSTRUMENT reported, because it was read through the same dead channel. A positive control on the subject is not a positive control on the observer.
